topicA.name: AI's Impact on Search and Content Strategy

resources.headline: From content creation to content orchestration: How agentic AI changes the role of content strategists.
resources.fullText: This article explores how agentic AI is transforming content creation into orchestration for strategists, detailing new responsibilities and essential human oversight.
keyNotes: Powerful computer programs, called "agentic AI," are changing how businesses create their online materials, like articles or videos.
Instead of just making content, these smart programs are helping companies "orchestrate" it, which means organizing and managing it like a conductor leads an orchestra.
This shift means that people who plan what content a company produces (called "strategists") will have new responsibilities in their jobs.
Even with these advanced computer programs doing more, it's still essential for humans to oversee and guide the entire process.
resources.question: The article mentions that advanced computer programs, or "agentic AI," will bring "new responsibilities" for those who plan content. In your own work, what new responsibilities might you take on if smart technology started handling some of your current tasks, and how would you ensure human oversight remains essential?

resources.headline: SEO budgets: Where to invest for maximum impact as search evolves.
resources.fullText: An analysis of optimal SEO budget allocation for evolving search landscapes, focusing on content and authority for AI search visibility.
keyNotes: The article explores the best ways companies should spend their money to get noticed when people search online, a process often called "SEO" (Search Engine Optimization).
It's especially important to rethink this spending because how people search online is constantly changing, which the article refers to as "evolving search landscapes."

To be easily found in these new search environments, particularly when artificial intelligence is involved ("AI search"), companies should focus their investment on creating valuable "content," meaning useful information.
Another crucial area for companies to put their money is in building "authority," which means establishing themselves as a trusted and reliable source of information.
resources.question: Given that online search is changing and AI is becoming more involved, how might the idea of building 'authority' and creating valuable 'content' apply to how you share information or build trust in your own professional field, even if it's not directly about marketing?

resources.headline: Getting Your Product Into ChatGPT Isn’t The Hard Part, Getting It Through Checkout Is via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
resources.fullText: I provide some pro bono consulting to a retailer located on the Upper East Side of New York City, and at our last video meeting, we covered some new ground. Structured data, catalog feeds, a connection to Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol or OpenAI’s Agentic Commerce Protocol. But we didn’t talk about what determines whether a sale happens: Once an AI agent, not a person, is the one completing the transaction, does the checkout underneath still work? Shopify President Harley Finkelstein answered part of that question on the company’s February 2026 earnings call, and the number is not small. Orders arriving through AI-powered search have grown 15 times since January 2025 and are already routing through three separate protocols built in the last year: Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol, OpenAI’s Agentic Commerce Protocol, and Salesforce’s Agentforce Commerce, which chose to align with UCP rather than build a competing standard. Etsy sellers went live inside ChatGPT first, with Shopify merchants including Glossier, Spanx, and Vuori following. OpenAI has since pulled back from native in-chat checkout, moving purchases into retailer apps instead, which makes the underlying question sharper rather than less relevant. I emailed Konstantin Klyagin to find out what happens after that. He founded QAwerk in 2015 to give software a proper testing partner, and the agency has since tested more than 300 client projects across North America, Europe, and Africa. His answer to the visibility question was getting a product surfaced in an AI platform’s results is the easy half, but most of the current friction sits downstream, in the part nobody is testing yet. An Agent Shops Nothing Like A Person Klyagin’s framing is simple once you hear it: A human shopper browses at an inconsistent pace, gets distracted, abandons a cart, and comes back to it hours later. An AI agent fires rapid, structured API calls, evaluates a product against the criteria it was given, and executes a decision in seconds. That speed is exactly what breaks systems tuned for humans. Rate limiting and bot detection exist to catch behavior that looks automated, which is precisely what a legitimate shopping agent looks like. Session logic built around one continuous human visit chokes on an agent that queries a product, closes the session, and returns later to finish the purchase. Klyagin’s team has tested multi-agent systems in other regulated industries and keeps finding the same root cause: Most QA plans verify whether a system produces the correct output, and almost none verify whether the surrounding infrastructure tolerates a non-human actor moving through it at machine speed. This is where a well-ranked, well-optimized product still fails to convert. The SEO, and AI-visibility work most retailers are focused on right now sits entirely upstream of it. The Failure Pattern Isn’t What You’d Guess I asked Klyagin for a real example of a checkout, product-data, or refund failure caused specifically by an AI agent, expecting a dramatic story. He hasn’t seen a verified production incident where an agent itself caused a client’s checkout to fail, and he was not willing to dress up an ordinary ecommerce bug as an agent failure and is exactly why his actual answer is worth more than a manufactured anecdote. What his team has found, repeatedly, is a subtler problem that becomes serious the moment the buyer is software instead of a person. On one client project, a funnel called Pridefit, engineers found that two separate components had been maintaining their own copies of the same plan data, with small differences in pricing, and attributes between the two. A human shopper might never notice, or might just refresh the page. An AI agent has no visual context and no judgment to fall back on. If it selects a plan based on one data source and checkout validates against the other, the mismatch in price, SKU, or availability can stall the transaction in a state the agent cannot resolve on its own. Klyagin’s team removed the duplication and centralized the plan data, so every part of the funnel pulled from one source. But the pattern he expects to see most often across agentic commerce generally is not an agent picking the wrong product. It’s systems disagreeing about the state of a purchase: An inventory feed says a variant is in stock while checkout says it’s sold out, a timed-out request gets retried against an endpoint that isn’t properly idempotent, or a refund clears on the merchant’s side before the updated order state ever reaches the agent that initiated it. A person can often shrug off an inconsistency like that and figure out what actually happened. An agent needs every API, every product feed, and every order status to already agree. 3 Checks Worth Running Before You Chase A Fourth Protocol Klyagin points clients toward three specific tests, and I think every retailer currently focused on catalog sync and structured markup should run all three before adding a fourth AI platform to the list. Load-test the checkout API the way an agent actually hits it. Not one slow human session at a time, but many parallel calls fired in quick succession. A checkout that has handled millions of human sessions without incident can still fail the first time it meets that traffic pattern, and most retailers connecting to UCP or ACP right now genuinely don’t know whether theirs will. Check product data accuracy the way a machine reads it, not the way a browser renders it. A page that looks perfectly consistent to a human visitor can be pulling from two disagreeing sources underneath, and an agent has no way to notice the gap the way a person scrolling the page might. Verify refunds and returns clear correctly on the first attempt. When a machine initiates the request, there’s no customer service rep in the loop to catch a partial failure or a status that never syncs back. None of these three requires waiting for UCP, ACP, or Agentforce Commerce to mature fur
keyNotes: It turns out that getting your product to appear in an AI like ChatGPT is actually the easy part; the real challenge is making sure the AI can successfully *buy* your product. This is because most online shopping systems are built for slow human shoppers, not super-fast AI agents.

Unlike people who browse slowly and get distracted, AI shopping agents make decisions and send requests incredibly fast, which can accidentally trigger website defenses designed to stop automated "bot" behavior. These systems often mistake legitimate AI shopping for harmful activity.

The biggest problem isn't AI picking the wrong item, but rather different parts of a company's own systems disagreeing about important details like price or whether an item is in stock. A human might notice these inconsistencies, but an AI agent gets stuck because it can't make judgment calls.

To get ready for AI shoppers, companies need to test their checkout systems by sending many fast requests at once, ensure all product information is perfectly consistent across their internal systems, and verify that refunds work correctly on the first try without human help.
resources.question: The article highlights that AI agents get stuck when different parts of a company's internal systems disagree about product details, like price or stock. Thinking about your own work, where might similar hidden inconsistencies exist in your processes or data that a human might overlook but a precise, fast-moving machine would immediately expose?

topicB.name: Data Quality and Signal Loss in B2B Marketing

resources.headline: Marketing without signals: How to perform when the data disappears
resources.fullText:
Navigating signal loss without losing momentum is a hurdle for every marketing leader. At the MarTech Conference we talked about building control with the data you already own.
The post Marketing without signals: How to perform when the data disappears appeared first on MarTech.
keyNotes: Marketing leaders are currently facing a big challenge where they can't easily track what customers are doing online, which is like losing their 'signals' or clues.
This difficulty in seeing customer behavior makes it tough for companies to keep their marketing efforts effective and moving forward.
At a major industry event called the MarTech Conference, experts discussed how to handle this problem of disappearing customer data.
One key solution suggested was for companies to focus on and make the most of the information they already have about their customers, rather than relying on new, hard-to-get data.
By using this existing information, businesses can gain better control over their marketing strategies, even when external data is scarce.
resources.question: If the 'signals' or easy-to-track information about your customers or audience suddenly became unavailable, what existing information or 'data you already own' could you use to still make smart decisions in your own work or business?

resources.headline: Your AI Doesn't Have an Intelligence Problem. It Has a Data Problem.
resources.fullText: Key Takeaways The report details that AI performance depends less on model sophistication and more on whether the underlying contact and customer data is accurate, complete and usable. Research cited in the story shows that poor first- and third-party data readiness limits AI ROI, while clean data helps marketers sharpen targeting and compound pipeline results. Quick answer: Artificial intelligence (AI) performance rises or falls on the data feeding it. Clean, well-acquired contacts sharpen targeting and compound pipeline. Noisy data scales your mistakes faster than any human could. The “Clean Data: The Engine Behind Every AI Motion” report proves that clean data isn’t back-office cleanup— it’s the engine behind every AI motion that moves pipeline. You’ve been sold a story about smarter models. Here’s the plot twist: the model rarely breaks. The data does. The report, sponsored by Convertr and published by Demand Gen Report, cuts through the AI hype with evidence from the people building and studying these systems. The key takeaway is feed AI accurate contacts and it tightens follow-up and compounds pipeline; feed it noise and out comes AI slop. Why Data Readiness Is the Crack in Your Foundation Start with the numbers: according to the CMO Council, 71% of marketing leaders rate their organization’s ability to use first-party customer data as ineffective or underdeveloped. Another 80% aren’t yet highly effective at sourcing and integrating third-party data. Read those figures back to back. Most teams can’t fully trust the data they own or the data they buy. That’s the crack in the foundation before AI ever enters the picture. “Before AI, bad data slowed marketers down. Today, it scales their mistakes,” said Natalie Cunningham, SVP of marketing at Data Axle. “Every AI initiative rises or falls on the quality of the data behind it.” What the Report Covers The report tackles four connected realities every B2B marketer needs to reckon with: The state of data readiness: Why the gap is wider than you think. What a contact really means: Why volume isn’t the edge you assume it is. AI-powered enrichment: How connected signals activate audiences faster. Data quality strategies: What separates teams reporting ROI from teams reporting excuses. The payoff for getting this right is measurable. The CMO Council found that organizations with stronger AI-human integration are nearly three times more likely to report measurable ROI from AI initiatives. Stop scaling the mess. Start compounding pipeline. Read the full report
keyNotes: It turns out that how well an Artificial Intelligence (AI) system works isn't mostly about how fancy the AI program is, but rather how good and clean the information (data) you feed it is.

A big challenge for businesses is that 71% of marketing leaders admit they aren't good at using the information they collect directly from customers, and 80% aren't effective at using information from other sources.
If you give an AI system messy or incorrect information, it won't just make small errors; it will actually make your mistakes bigger and faster than any person could.

The article highlights that companies that are better at combining AI tools with human effort are almost three times more likely to see real, measurable benefits (like making more money) from their AI projects.
resources.question: The article warns that 'noisy data scales your mistakes faster than any human could.' Thinking about the information you use in your own role, what steps could you take to ensure that any new tools or systems you adopt don't just amplify existing problems, but instead help you succeed?

resources.headline: 96% of B2B marketers use AI, but hiring is moving toward judgment and QA roles
resources.fullText: 96% of B2B marketers use AI, but hiring is moving toward judgment and QA roles  marketscale.com
keyNotes: Almost all (96%) of people who market products or services from one business to another business (that's what 'B2B' means) are now using Artificial Intelligence (AI).
Even though AI is widely used, companies are looking to hire people for jobs that require human thinking and checking work.
Specifically, new jobs are focusing on 'judgment' – meaning making smart decisions – and 'QA' (Quality Assurance), which is about making sure things are correct and high-quality.
This suggests that while machines handle some tasks, human skills like critical thinking and ensuring accuracy are becoming more valuable in the workplace.
resources.question: Given that almost all businesses are using AI, but still need human judgment and quality checks, where do you see the most important human skills fitting into your own work or industry as technology advances?
